definition: The consumer or business that holds the card and authorizes the payment.
The party selling goods or services and accepting the card as payment.
The bank that issues the card, owns the cardholder relationship, extends the credit or holds the deposits, and approves or declines each authorization.
The bank licensed by the networks to accept card transactions on a merchant's behalf and deposit the proceeds into the merchant's account.
Visa, Mastercard, Amex or Discover: routes messages between acquirer and issuer, sets interchange and the operating rules, and runs settlement.
The standard open-loop structure, with the card network in the middle moving messages and money between the issuer and the acquirer.

short: The network is also the bank
definition: A closed structure where one company is network, issuer and acquirer at once, so it sets its own pricing. Amex and Discover began this way.

short: Works anywhere the network is taken
definition: A card usable at any merchant that accepts the network, because the network connects many issuers to many acquirers.
A card accepted only by the issuing brand or a defined group, such as a store gift card, with no network in the middle.
The technology company that formats, transmits and reconciles transaction messages between the merchant, the acquirer, the network and the issuer.
Runs the authorization logic, balance checks and card records for an issuer, often for programs the bank does not build itself.
Handles authorization routing, capture, settlement files and merchant funding on an acquirer's behalf.
Takes card details from a website or app, encrypts them and passes the transaction to the processor. Mostly a card-not-present concept.
A PayFac holds one master merchant account and onboards many sub-merchants underneath it, taking on their underwriting and risk.
A business that accepts cards through a payment facilitator's master account rather than holding its own merchant account.

context: ISO; Mastercard calls it an MSP
definition: An ISO signs merchants up for card acceptance on behalf of an acquiring bank and is paid out of the merchant's processing fees.

short: Who is legally on the hook
definition: The entity that appears on the cardholder's statement and carries the legal and financial responsibility for the transaction, including refunds and chargebacks.
A licensed network member that lets a fintech or program manager issue or acquire under its membership, and stays accountable to the network for it.
Handles the product, customer experience and day-to-day operations of a card program that sits on a sponsor bank's BIN.
An ISV builds business software and embeds payment acceptance into it, often earning a share of the processing revenue.
The terminal, register or software that captures the card and starts the transaction. Abbreviated POS.
Apple Pay, Google Pay and similar: hold a tokenized version of the card and present it over NFC or online.
The party, usually the network, that swaps a real card number for a token and can map it back for the issuer.

short: A bank licensed by the scheme
definition: Only licensed members may issue or acquire directly; everyone else reaches the network through one.
Software that lets a merchant send transactions to several processors or gateways and switch or retry between them.

short: Ask the issuer: yes or no
definition: A real-time request to the issuer to confirm the card is valid and the funds or credit are available. It reserves the amount but moves no money.
The acquirer submits the completed transaction and the network passes the record to the issuer, calculating what each side owes. Still no money has moved.
The actual transfer of funds between issuer and acquirer through the network's settlement accounts.
The acquirer deposits the settled proceeds, less fees, into the merchant's bank account. Usually a day or two after the sale.
The merchant tells the acquirer to collect a previously authorized amount, normally when the goods actually ship or the tab is closed.
The issuer reduces the cardholder's available balance by the authorized amount while waiting for the capture. It expires if never captured.
Captured transactions grouped and submitted for clearing in one file, traditionally at the end of the merchant's day.
The cut-off at which a merchant submits its batch. Miss it and funding slips a day.
An authorization taken before the final amount is known, as at a hotel check-in or a fuel pump.
An additional authorization that raises an existing hold, used when a hotel stay or a bar tab grows.
The issuer approves less than requested because that is all the balance covers, letting the cardholder settle the rest another way. Common on prepaid.
A message releasing a hold before it is captured, so the cardholder's available balance recovers straight away.
Cancelling a captured transaction while it is still in the open batch, so it never reaches clearing and never shows as a refund.
A separate transaction returning funds to the cardholder after the original one settled. It does not undo the original.
A forced reversal initiated by the issuer after a cardholder dispute, pulling funds from the merchant and putting the burden of proof on them.
The merchant supplies evidence contesting a chargeback and re-presents the transaction to the issuer.
When issuer and merchant cannot resolve a dispute, the network rules on it and charges the loser a fee.
An attempt to settle a dispute between issuer and acquirer before it goes to the network for a binding decision.

short: The network answers for the issuer
definition: When the issuer cannot be reached, the network approves or declines on its behalf within limits the issuer set in advance.
A transaction where the card is dipped, tapped or swiped, so the terminal reads the chip or stripe. Lower risk, lower interchange.
Online, in-app, phone or mail transactions where the card cannot be read. Higher fraud risk and higher interchange.
A card-not-present transaction taken by post or over the phone, with the details keyed in by the merchant.
A card the merchant has saved with the cardholder's agreement, used for repeat or one-click purchases.
A repeating charge on a stored card, such as a subscription, flagged so the issuer treats it differently from a fresh purchase.
The short code the issuer returns on approval, quoted later to tie a settled transaction back to its authorization.
Submitting a transaction for clearing without a matching online authorization, using a code obtained another way. Carries extra liability.

short: Do not spend what has not arrived
definition: Settling only once money is actually in hand, rather than advancing it and taking the risk.
The fee, set by the network, that the acquirer pays the issuer on each transaction. It is the largest part of what a merchant pays and it funds rewards and issuer risk.
A fee the network charges on processed volume for use of its rails and brand. Small next to interchange, and paid by the acquirer.
The total a merchant pays per transaction: interchange, plus assessments, plus the processor's markup.
Pricing that passes interchange and assessments straight through and adds a disclosed margin. The most transparent model.
A single blended rate on every transaction regardless of card type. Simple, predictable, usually more expensive on average.
Pricing that sorts transactions into a few buckets whose definitions the processor controls. Opaque, and easy to downgrade into the expensive tier.
A transaction that fails to meet the conditions for the interchange category it could have qualified for, and costs more as a result.
The unit card pricing is quoted in. 100 bps is 1%.
Tax and customer reference data supplied on commercial card transactions to qualify for lower interchange.
Full line-item data on a commercial card transaction, which unlocks the lowest interchange for business and government spend.
A US rule capping debit interchange for large issuers and requiring that merchants have a choice of at least two unaffiliated debit networks.
Debit cards from issuers over the Durbin asset threshold, whose interchange is capped. Unregulated debit, from small issuers, is not.
Choosing between the debit networks available on a card to minimize the merchant's cost.

short: A fee for paying by card
definition: An extra amount added to the price for card payment. Permitted only within network rules and where local law allows.
A fee for using a particular payment channel rather than for using a card as such, allowed in narrower circumstances than a surcharge.
Advertising a card price and discounting for cash, which achieves a similar result to surcharging under different rules.
Funds the acquirer withholds from a merchant against future chargebacks or failure to deliver.
A reserve that keeps a set percentage of recent volume, releasing each tranche after an agreed period.
A fixed fee the acquirer charges the merchant for handling a dispute, usually payable whatever the outcome.
Funding the merchant the full transaction amount and invoicing fees separately, rather than netting them off.
Funding the merchant the transaction amount less fees, so the deposit is already net.
The economic benefit of holding funds between the moment they are collected and the moment they are paid out.
An arrangement where a partner such as an ISV or ISO receives an agreed portion of the processing revenue it introduces.
Supplying the data and settling within the windows that let each transaction reach the lowest interchange category available to it.
The Primary Account Number embossed or printed on the card, 13 to 19 digits, which identifies the issuer and the account.
The Bank Identification Number at the start of the PAN, identifying the issuer, the network, the country and the product type. Now formally the IIN.
A checksum over the card number that detects most mistyped digits. It proves nothing about whether the account exists.
The month and year the card stops working, after which the issuer reissues. Used as a light verification field online.
The code printed on the card, not stored on the chip or stripe, used to suggest the card was in hand for a card-not-present sale.
A separate verification value carried on the chip, different from the one on the magnetic stripe, so stripe data copied from a chip will not work.
The magnetic stripe's encoded fields: the PAN, expiry, service code and a verification value. Copying it is how counterfeit cards were made.
The magnetic band on the back. It presents the same data every time, which is exactly why skimming worked.
The chip that computes a unique cryptogram per transaction, so intercepted data cannot be replayed. Named for Europay, Mastercard and Visa.

short: Proof the real chip was there
definition: A one-time value the chip generates from transaction data and a secret key, which the issuer verifies. An ARQC is the authorization request cryptogram.
The AID that tells the terminal which payment application on the chip to use, for example debit or credit on the same card.
The CVM: PIN, signature, on-device biometric or nothing at all. The chip and terminal negotiate which to use from a priority list.
Presenting the card or phone over NFC. Uses the same chip cryptography as a dip, so it is not the security step back that swiping was.
Three digits in the track data saying where the card is valid, whether a chip must be used, and what verification is required.

short: A card number that is not the card number
definition: A network-issued substitute PAN, restricted to a merchant or device, which keeps working when the underlying card is reissued.
PAR: a non-sensitive value linking every token and the real PAN for the same account, so a merchant can recognize a returning customer without holding card data.
A network service that pushes new card numbers and expiry dates to merchants holding cards on file, so subscriptions survive reissues.
A card number generated for online or in-app use, often with limits on amount, merchant or lifetime.
A virtual card that expires after a single transaction, so a leak from the merchant is worthless.
A card drawing on funds loaded in advance rather than a deposit account or a credit line.
A card that draws directly on the cardholder's own bank balance, usually with lower interchange than credit.
A card drawing on a revolving credit line, where the issuer takes the credit risk and earns interest as well as interchange.
A card with no revolving balance: the whole amount falls due each cycle.
Corporate, purchasing and fleet cards, which carry richer data requirements and their own interchange categories.
Encoding the chip, printing the number and loading the keys that make a blank card belong to one account.

short: The rules for handling card data
definition: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: the controls anyone storing, processing or transmitting card data must meet, set by the networks jointly.
Every system that touches card data. Shrinking it, by never letting raw card data into your systems, is the cheapest way to reduce compliance burden.
The SAQ: the form smaller merchants complete to attest to PCI compliance, instead of a full on-site assessment.
A QSA is certified by the PCI Council to assess and attest to a company's compliance.

short: Swap the number for a stand-in
definition: Replacing card data with a token that is useless if stolen, and can only be mapped back by the token service. The main tool for cutting PCI scope.
P2PE encrypts card data inside the terminal before it reaches the merchant's systems, so those systems never hold readable card data.
An HSM is tamper-resistant hardware that stores cryptographic keys and performs PIN and cryptogram operations without ever exposing the keys.
Derived Unique Key Per Transaction: each transaction is encrypted with its own key derived from a base key, so compromising one reveals nothing about the others.
3DS adds an issuer authentication step to a card-not-present payment, and in return usually shifts fraud liability from the merchant to the issuer.
The rules deciding whether the merchant or the issuer bears a fraudulent transaction. It moves with technology: EMV for card-present, 3DS for online.
From the 2015 US milestone, the party that failed to support chip, merchant or issuer, bears counterfeit fraud losses.
AVS compares the numeric parts of the billing address against the issuer's record. A weak signal on its own, useful combined with others.
A control that flags or blocks unusual bursts of activity on a card, device or account.
Attackers running small or zero-value authorizations to find which stolen card numbers still work, often against a merchant's own checkout.

short: Guessing the rest of the number
definition: Generating candidate card numbers from a known BIN and testing them until some authorize.
A device on a terminal or ATM that reads and stores magnetic stripe data for later counterfeiting.
A thin device between chip and reader that captures chip data. Far less useful to an attacker, because the cryptogram cannot be replayed.
A cardholder disputing a transaction they actually made, whether by mistake or deliberately. Often indistinguishable from real fraud at first.

short: The real account, the wrong person
definition: An attacker gaining control of a legitimate account and transacting as the cardholder.
KYC: verifying the identity of a person before opening an account, required by anti-money-laundering rules.
KYB: the equivalent checks on a business, its ownership and its beneficial owners, done when onboarding a merchant.
AML: the programme of monitoring, screening and reporting that regulated firms must run.
Screening parties against US sanctions lists before doing business with them.

short: Deciding whether to take the risk
definition: Assessing a merchant's business model, financials and chargeback exposure before granting acceptance, and setting reserves accordingly.
The long-standing message format for card authorizations, with numbered fields and a message type indicator. Still what most card traffic speaks.
An XML-based messaging standard with far more structured data, replacing older formats across wires and real-time payments.
The MTI: four digits at the head of an ISO 8583 message saying what it is. 0100 is an authorization request, 0110 its response.
Authorization and clearing sent as separate messages, which is what allows tips, partial captures and delayed shipping. The credit card norm.
One message that both authorizes and clears, typical of PIN debit, where the amount is final at the moment of sale.
A debit transaction authenticated by PIN and routed over a debit network, usually cheaper for the merchant than signature debit.
The ARN assigned during clearing, used to trace a specific transaction between acquirer, network and issuer, especially in disputes.
The RRN carried in the authorization message, used to match an authorization to its later clearing record.
The file the network produces telling each member what it owes or is owed once the day's transactions are netted.
Matching authorizations, captures, settlement files and bank deposits against each other to find what is missing or wrong.
A hold visible to the cardholder that has reduced available balance but has not yet hit the statement.
A temporary entry the issuer makes on authorization, replaced by the real posting when clearing arrives.
The Automated Clearing House: low-cost batched bank transfers used for payroll, bills and merchant funding. Days, not seconds, and reversible.
ACH processed in same-day windows rather than overnight, at a higher fee and within a value cap.
A real-time, individually processed bank transfer that is effectively irrevocable once sent.
The RTP network: bank-to-bank transfers that clear and settle in seconds, around the clock, and cannot be reversed.
The US Federal Reserve's real-time payment service, launched in 2023 as an alternative to RTP.
An OCT sends funds to a card rather than pulling them, which is how payouts and instant transfers to a debit card work.
An AFT pulls money from a card to fund an account or wallet, and is flagged so the issuer knows it is not a purchase.
A payment the payer initiates, like a wire or an OCT. Hard to reverse, so a favourite of scammers.
A payment the payee initiates against permission given earlier, like a card charge or an ACH debit. Reversible, which is why disputes exist.
The binding operating regulations every member agrees to, covering acceptance, disputes, branding, data and fees.
Sharing bank account data and initiating payments through APIs with the account holder's consent, rather than by screen scraping.
